Concept
Planetary orbits are ellipses with the Sun at a focus, traversed at varying speed.

Where on its orbit does Mercury move fastest? Which orbit is least circular?

Units
Distances in AU, time in years, so GM☉ = 4π² AU³/yr². Speed converted to km/s for display (1 AU/yr ≈ 4.74 km/s). Full-system view: spacing between orbits is compressed for legibility; each orbit's shape, eccentricity, and Sun-at-focus placement are exact.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Orient yourself

The yellow disk at the center is the Sun. The colored dots are planets, and their orbits are traced in from the analytic ellipse so you can see them at rest.

The label on the canvas notes the convention: distances are to scale; planet icons are enlarged so you can see them. Otherwise the planets would be invisible dots.

Press ▶ Play (or Start below) to set them in motion. Watch one full orbit of Mercury.

2 · Predict — where is Mercury fastest?

The simulation is paused so you can commit before you observe. Along its orbit, where do you think Mercury moves fastest?

3 · Observe — the speed readout

Now watch Mercury. The stats panel shows its instantaneous distance r and speed v. Notice how v is largest when r is smallest, and smallest when r is largest.

Closest approach (perihelion) is where it moves fastest — Kepler's second law in action.

4 · Predict — the shape

Look at each orbit and ask where the Sun sits inside it — dead centre, or off to one side? Click a planet to read its eccentricity e in the stats panel. Which orbit is least circular?

5 · Resolve

Every orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. Most look circular because e is tiny; Mercury (e = 0.206) is the only one where the Sun sits visibly off-centre.

Along each ellipse the planet speeds up near perihelion and slows near aphelion — Kepler's second law.

03

One gravity law sets every orbit

Each planet is pulled toward the Sun with an acceleration that falls off as the inverse square of its distance r:

a = −GM r̂ / r²
r̂ is the unit vector pointing from the Sun to the planet, and GM is the Sun's gravitational parameter.

The sim measures distance in astronomical units (AU) and time in years, which makes GM = 4π² AU³/yr². At 1 AU the pull is about 39.5 AU/yr², or 5.9 × 10⁻³ m/s². The sim steps this law forward in time for each planet, starting from that planet's real a and e.

See itRun the Inner view at a faster time rate. Watch for: each planet returning to where it started after one lap, with the inner ones lapping the outer ones.
04

A planet moves fastest nearest the Sun

A planet's speed is not constant. Energy conservation under the Sun's gravity gives the speed at any distance r, for an orbit of semi-major axis a:

v² = GM (2/r − 1/a)

Smaller r gives larger v. Mercury moves at 58.98 km/s at its closest approach, 0.308 AU, and 38.86 km/s at its farthest, 0.467 AU. The speed ratio, 1.52, equals the ratio of the farthest to the closest distance.

This is Kepler's second law: the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. In 0.01 yr, Mercury sweeps 0.0191 AU² both near its closest point and near its farthest.

See itHighlight Mercury and run at 1×. Watch for: v (now) largest when r (now) is smallest, and smallest when it is largest.
05

The Sun sits at one focus of each ellipse

Each orbit is an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. With θ measured from the closest point:

r(θ) = a(1 − e²) / (1 + e cos θ)
The closest distance is a(1 − e) and the farthest is a(1 + e).

The Sun is ae from the ellipse's centre. For Mercury, e = 0.206 puts it 0.080 AU off-centre, about a fifth of a. For Earth, e = 0.017 gives only 0.017 AU. Mercury has the largest e of the eight, and Mars is next at 0.093.

Look for the off-centre Sun, not a squashed shape. Mercury's orbit is only 2% shorter than it is wide, since b/a = √(1 − e²) = 0.979.

See itHighlight Mercury and look at its orbit. Watch for: the Sun off-centre in Mercury's orbit, and e = 0.206 in the panel.
06

A larger orbit takes longer to complete

In the sim's units, the time T of one lap, in years, and the semi-major axis a, in AU, obey T² = a³. This is Kepler's third law, and it holds here because GM = 4π².

Planeta (AU)T (yr)
Mercury0.3870.241
Earth1.0001.000
Mars1.5241.881
Neptune30.06164.8

The sim has no period readout. You can still see it: Mercury completes about 4.15 laps in one Earth year.

See itRun the Inner view at 8×. Watch for: Mercury completing about four laps while Earth completes one.
07

Where it matters

  • Mission planning. The relation v² = GM(2/r − 1/a) gives a spacecraft's speed at any point on its orbit around the Sun.
  • Comets. Halley's comet has e ≈ 0.97, far beyond any planet here. Its speed at closest approach is about 60 times its speed at the farthest point, since the ratio is (1 + e)/(1 − e).
  • JEE problems. Angular momentum m r v⊥ is conserved for any orbit under a central force, and T² ∝ a³ applies to any bodies orbiting one central mass.
Go deeper

Gravity points straight at the Sun, so it exerts no torque about the Sun, and r v⊥ stays constant. That is the equal-areas law, because the area swept per unit time is half of r v⊥.

08

Summary

In one line. The sim moves all eight planets under the Sun's gravity and shows each one's distance and speed as it goes.

Key points

  • Speed is highest at the closest point to the Sun and lowest at the farthest.
  • The Sun sits at one focus of each elliptical orbit, off the centre by ae.
  • T² = a³ in AU and years, though the sim shows no period readout.

Common mix-ups

  • "A planet moves at constant speed on a circle." Its speed changes along the orbit, and the orbit is an ellipse.
  • "A planet slows down as it nears the Sun." It speeds up, because it is falling inward.
  • "A large e means a very flat ellipse." It means the Sun is far off-centre. Even Mercury's orbit is only 2% shorter than wide.

Things to try on your own

  • Highlight each inner planet in turn and record the largest and smallest v (now).
  • Switch to Full view and find the orbit whose Sun looks most off-centre.
  • Run at 8× and count Venus laps against Earth laps.
